lesson_title: The Payslip and the Report Card
hook_text: Two families on one street. One earns more every year. The other lives better. Which country do you want to be?
clip_script: Two families, one street. Family one: income up every single year — overtime, second job, a lodger in the back room. The payslip says WINNING. Now walk inside. The eldest left school when the fees ran out. The youngest coughs all winter because the clinic queue defeats a working mother. Nobody sleeps well — the street isn't safe. Money up. Life, not. Family two earns less, and it barely moves. But the kids are in school and staying there. Everyone's on the clinic's books. The stokvel bought the burglar bars. Supper happens together. Payslip: standing still. Lives: moving. That's the difference between GROWTH and DEVELOPMENT — the payslip versus the report card — and countries carry both. Growth is real GDP, and here's the trick everyone misses: divide it by the number of mouths. A payslip growing slower than the family is a pay cut wearing a smile — and that has been South Africa's last decade. Development is the report card the UN actually grades: how long people live, how much they learn, what they can afford. The exam question, and honestly the national question, is the same: never ask only is the country richer. Ask — is anybody living better?
visual_style: A split-screen street: one house stacking coins in the window while its rooms dim, the other house lit room by room — schoolbooks, clinic card, supper table — while a payslip and a report card hover above each roof.
mood: Warm, human, landing a serious question softly.
pacing: Two measured household portraits, a sharp pivot at the divide-by-mouths trick, reflective close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take growth, development, both policy toolkits and the north-south divide into the big Paper 1 essay.
